payload.content:
A short read · [sn_reading_time]

Music has a recognition problem. Another list isn't the answer.

A short read on why most of the people who make records have nobody to vouch for them.

Read the full research paper →

Jump to: The setup · The analogy · What the framework is · Why this matters · The shift · The economics of recognition

Section 1

The setup

A songwriter registers with a performing rights organization and acquires an identity the royalty system can act on. A session drummer who has played on two hundred records under a name no organization has registered acquires nothing. Both made the work. Only one of them is legible to the infrastructure that pays for it.

This usually gets described as a coverage problem, as though the unaffiliated contributor were waiting for adoption to reach them. The description is wrong in a way that matters. Institutions in the current rights infrastructure are not a delivery mechanism for standing that exists independently of them. They are constitutive of it. Recognition by a society is what makes a claim legible, and a contributor outside every society is not under-served but absent.

Every cryptographic provenance system built so far inherits that assumption. A signed work verifies against a published key, and the argument holds. It holds only after somebody has established that the key belongs to the person claiming it. Where that establishing happens, the answer is always an institution.

Much of the work in music is done by people no organization has registered.

Section 2

The analogy

Consider a job site.

Some of the people on it hold a license. A licensed electrician is authoritative about electrical work in the state that licensed them, and silent about plumbing, and silent about the state next door. A license issued somewhere larger does not carry further. It carries somewhere else. Scope is what a license supplies, and scope is not a quantity.

Most of the people on the site hold no license from anyone. What they have instead is a decade of finished work and a dozen people who will say so. Nobody confuses that for a license, and nobody pretends it is worth nothing.

Neither one is a permission slip for the other. They answer different questions, and a job site that only counted licenses would have to pretend most of its workforce was not there.

Music counts only the licenses. The unaffiliated contributor and the contributor with no record at all return the same result, which is nothing, and the system cannot tell them apart.

A held list: someone decides who is on it
A bounded roster of entries with three figures standing outside its edge. Whoever maintains the list decides who appears on it, and everyone outside returns the same empty result as someone with no record at all.

A held list
Someone decides who is on it

Two tracks: neither outranks the other
Two parallel lanes. The left lane carries a single sealed mark bounded by a bracket, standing for an attestation authoritative within a named scope. The right lane carries a rising series of bars, standing for a record that accrues from work done over time.

Two tracks
Neither outranks the other

Section 3

What the framework is

Four commitments define a standing framework worth building.

Scope is the primitive. An attestation is authoritative over a named right in a named territory and carries no weight anywhere else. A society holding a statutory authorization is fully authoritative inside it whatever its size, and silent outside it whatever its size. Membership counts and annual collections describe a body and say nothing about whether its attestation is true. Grading institutions would put magnitude back into the one layer where scope is the only thing that operates.

Standing runs on two tracks that never compete. The institutional track reads authority that already exists outside the framework. The accrued track computes weight from a record the contributor generated themselves, from attestations that are binary and from persistence that accumulates through signed work over time. A contributor may hold both, either, or neither, and the accrued track is independently sufficient. Institutional silence is not evidence.

Recognition comes from outside. Where a body holds a statutory, regulatory, or treaty-conferred authorization, recognition is a lookup against public records that other parties already maintain. Everything else, including trade associations, academies, guilds, and informal peer networks, is recognized by the verifying party rather than by the framework. A verifier is a platform, a society, a licensee, or a court, and every one of them already keeps a trust policy. Stating it asks them to write down something they have.

The computation is deterministic. The same record under the same stated policy produces the same weight for any party who runs it. Nothing is estimated, nothing is inferred, and the framework holds no belief about anything it cannot observe. A framework that answered an authorship question with a degree of belief would have undone the argument the two prior papers spent their length making.

What the framework holds is a composition rule and a way of recording conflict. What it declines to hold is a list, a score, a threshold, or an opinion about who counts. Where two attestations collide, it records the collision and leaves the resolution to whoever holds the authority to decide.

Section 4

Why this matters

Three groups feel the consequences differently.

For contributors nobody has registered. A session player outside union jurisdiction, an engineer with no certifying body, a producer working under a handle: each of them has a substantial record and no institution positioned to vouch for it. Under this framework their record accrues weight from the work itself, and no verifier's recognition set reduces it. Zero stops being a verdict and goes back to being a report on an empty record.

For societies, unions, and academies. They stop being the only door and lose nothing they actually hold. A society attesting that it represents a contributor for performing rights in a territory has said something true and bounded, and the framework reads that authorization rather than grading the body behind it. The small authorized society is authoritative within its scope. So is the large one, within its own.

For platforms, licensees, and courts. Every party that decides something consequential about a contributor already maintains a trust policy, usually undocumented and never inspectable. Stating a recognized issuer set converts an implicit policy into one that can be audited, and makes an anomalous change to it something an observer can see.

The win isn't routing institutions out of music. It's that the people who did the work stop depending on institutional recognition to be visible at all.

Section 5

The shift

The choice is between two questions.

The current infrastructure asks: "Who vouches for you?" For most of the people who make records the answer is nobody, and the cost of that answer is paid by whoever did the work and cannot be named.

The framework asks: "What have you done, who has said so, and under whose recognition?" That question has an answer for anyone who has worked, because persistence accrues from the work alone and needs no issuer to have spoken.

One of these has something to return for a session drummer. The other returns the same empty result it returns for a name that was invented this morning.

Weight computed this way is relative to the verifier who stated the policy, and two contributors are comparable only under a shared recognition set. No absolute ranking exists, and none is available. Producing one would require a universal recognition authority, which is the structure this whole argument runs against.

Section 6

The economics of recognition

Every proposal to fix this ends at a list, and a list has a price the proposal rarely names.

A list requires a maintainer. A maintainer requires criteria, criteria require a body to set them, and that body requires admission rules, an appeals process, and funding. At that point the fix has reproduced the institutional apparatus it was built to make unnecessary, and whoever ends up running it holds the power to grant and withhold standing.

A scoring function costs the same and hides more. Replacing the list with a formula looks like removing the discretion. Someone still selects the inputs, someone still weights them, someone still decides the shape of the curve. What changes is visibility: a list announces that a choice was made and invites argument, while a formula presents the same choice as measurement and lends the result an authority the underlying judgment has not earned.

A lookup costs nothing and scales with nobody. Determining whether a body holds a statutory authorization means consulting records that legislatures and supervising authorities already publish and already maintain. No new body, no new criteria, no new funding. Asking a verifier to state the issuers it already trusts is a comparable ask, because the policy exists and is merely unwritten.

Music already runs without an apex. Territorial societies hold overlapping authorizations, coordinate through reciprocal agreements, and answer to their own supervising authorities. There is no supreme center now and there has not been one for a century. What this framework declines to do is add one.

One apex: a root everyone must pass through
A single node at the top connected downward to four nodes below it. Every decision routes through the node at the top, which is the structure a framework-held list would create.

One apex
A root everyone passes through

Overlapping authority: scopes that meet without a center
Three intersecting circles of equal size, each representing a body authoritative within its own scope. They overlap at their edges and no circle contains the others, which is how music rights are already arranged.

Overlapping authority
Scopes that meet without a center
